content: The document titled Updated Recommendations on HIV Prevention, Infant Diagnosis, Antiretroviral Initiation, and Monitoring was published in March 2021 by the World Health Organization (WHO). It provides updated guidelines on various aspects of HIV care and prevention. 1. Definitions of Key Terms: HIV: Refers to the human immunodeficiency virus, with two types: HIV-1 (responsible for most global infections) and HIV-2. Acute HIV Infection: The period between initial infection and the detection of HIV antibodies. Age Groups: Adults are individuals older than 19 years, adolescents are aged 10–19 years, children are aged 1–9 years, and infants are younger than 1 year. Key Populations: Groups at high risk of HIV, including men who have sex with men, people who inject drugs, sex workers, transgender individuals, and people in prisons. Vulnerable Populations: Groups at risk in specific contexts, such as children, adolescents, orphans, people with disabilities, and migrant workers. 5. HIV Testing and Prevention: Combination Prevention: A strategy combining behavioral, biomedical, and structural approaches to reduce HIV transmission. Infant Diagnosis: Testing infants and children for HIV following potential exposure during pregnancy, delivery, or postpartum. Early infant diagnosis (before two months of age) is critical for timely treatment. Point-of-Care Testing: Conducted at the site of clinical care, with same-day results to facilitate immediate clinical decisions. Pre-Exposure Prophylaxis (PrEP): The use of antiretroviral drugs by HIV-negative individuals to prevent infection. 6. Antiretroviral Therapy (ART): ART: Refers to the use of a combination of three or more antiretroviral drugs to treat HIV infection. Viral Suppression: Achieving an undetectable viral load (≤50 copies/mL). Virological Failure: Defined as a persistent viral load >1,000 copies/mL after at least six months of ART. 7. Service Delivery: Adherence: The extent to which a person follows agreed recommendations, such as taking medication or changing lifestyle. Retention in Care: The percentage of individuals living with HIV who remain in care and on ART during a specified follow-up period. Public Health Approach: Focuses on population-level health needs, ensuring broad access to high-quality services and medicines through simplified and standardized approaches. 8. Acknowledgments: WHO acknowledges the contributions of numerous individuals and organizations to the development of these guidelines, including experts, clinicians, researchers, and representatives from various countries and institutions. This document serves as a comprehensive guide for healthcare providers, policymakers, and stakeholders involved in HIV prevention, diagnosis, treatment, and care. It emphasizes evidence-based practices, equity in access to care, and the importance of addressing the needs of key and vulnerable populations.
